CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: pancreas

0 of 6 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 2 fall below it; 4 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

Glutamine (free) — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 2.00 mM typical (1.5-4 mM (estimated)) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: From total free amino acid pool = 16.4 mM in rat pancreas (PMID 3362844). Glutamine typically ~12% of tissue free amino acid pools. 12% of 16.4 = 2.0 mM. Order-of-magnitude estimate. Each glutamine has one amide -NH2 and one alpha-amino -NH3+ group (total ~3 exchangeable protons).

Robustness to input uncertainty: upper-bound only

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (side-chain amide NH2 [amide]: concentration 1.5-4 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.01-0.05%, 1.5 T: 0.02-0.15%, 3 T: 0.02-0.31%, 5 T: 0.03-0.45%, 7 T: 0.04-0.53%. Threshold 0.5%. The point estimate is below threshold; only the high corner clears it.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • At 0.5 T: glutamine amide (+3.5 ppm in simulation) overlaps with ascorbic acid hydroxyl (+1.0 ppm): separation 53 Hz < combined exchange-broadened linewidth ~138 Hz. This collision resolves at higher fields. At all fields: overlap with semisolid MT pool is universal and not specific to glutamine.
  • If the true shift is ~2.2 ppm rather than 3.5 ppm, the collision with ascorbic acid at 0.5 T would be less severe (larger ppm gap) but the proximity to water would increase, worsening direct saturation issues.

Direct water saturation: At the simulated offset (3.5 ppm) and optimized B1 values, direct saturation bandwidth (21-64 Hz) is well below the offset (>200 Hz at all fields). Direct water saturation is not a concern for this pool. However, if the true shift is ~2.2 ppm, direct saturation spillover becomes more relevant at low fields.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: The side-chain amide kex (65.5 s⁻¹, range 15-158) is a class-level amide value borrowed from brain (human in vivo, PMID 40228056 and 23008121) — no pancreas-specific measurement. Exchange rates from brain may not apply to pancreas due to different pH (~7.2 vs ~7.4), temperature, and macromolecular environment. The large kex spread produces a 4-14× contrast range that highlights the uncertainty.

Note: For the amide regime (kex ~65 s⁻¹, slow exchange at all fields), the swept B1 of 0.5-0.75 µT is typical. MTRasym or Lorentzian difference analysis would be appropriate. AREX removes T1/direct-saturation bias and could improve specificity at higher fields. Multi-pool fitting would be needed to separate from semisolid MT background.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

amine CEST (~3.0 ppm): 0 CEST/NOE application and 3 metabolite-change studies verified (3 human, 0 animal; 216 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). No glutamine CEST in pancreas. Glutamine is among the top 5 most-reported altered metabolites in PDAC metabolomics (systematic review of 25 studies). Serum glutamine is lower in PDAC vs benign disease (n=56) but higher in CA19-9-high vs CA19-9-normal PDAC (n=103). Glutamine metabolism is a therapeutic target (GLS inhibitors). Strong rationale for CEST but not yet applied.

Caveats / critique (5 points, 243 words) — Concentration 2.0 mM (range 1.5-4.0) is plausible for free glutamine in pancreas but no specific MRS citation was provided. Glutamine is a key metabolite in pan…
  • Concentration 2.0 mM (range 1.5-4.0) is plausible for free glutamine in pancreas but no specific MRS citation was provided. Glutamine is a key metabolite in pancreatic amino acid handling. I agree with Agent 2's identification of two exchangeable groups: alpha-ammonium (amine) and side-chain amide NH2 (amide). The amide classification is correct.
  • HOWEVER, Agent 2 states the side-chain amide shifts at ~2.2 ppm while the simulation used 3.5 ppm (the generic class-level median for 'amide protons'). Glutamine's side-chain amide in solution NMR is at ~2.1-2.3 ppm, NOT at 3.5 ppm (which is protein backbone amide). This is a significant mismatch. The simulated shift may be ~1.2-1.4 ppm too far downfield.
  • The simulation used 3.5 ppm (generic amide class value). The actual glutamine side-chain amide chemical shift is ~2.1-2.3 ppm in solution NMR. No in vivo pancreas measurement available to confirm the exact offset. None — both exchangeable groups (alpha-ammonium and side-chain amide) were identified.
  • Groups not simulated: alpha-ammonium NH3+ [amine] -- the reference table has no verified exchange rate and shift for amine protons -- we don't know; not simulated no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Estimate only.
  • Each glutamine bears ~3 exchangeable protons (2 from amide, 1 from alpha-amino). [Unsourced reasoning] 1 numeric step(s) rest on an unsourced assumption: 'Glutamine estimated as ~12% of total free amino acid pool'.

Frequency-collision analysis: At 0.5 T: ascorbic acid (+1.0 ppm) overlaps with glutamine amide (+3.5 ppm): separation 53 Hz < combined linewidth ~138 Hz. This collision is specific to the simulated 3.5 ppm shift for glutamine; if glutamine's true shift is ~2.2 ppm, the collision may not occur. At all fields: overlap with semisolid MT pool (universal). The hydroxyl offset at 1.0 ppm is very close to water, making direct saturation a greater concern than collisions with other metabolites.

Direct water saturation:

  • At 0.5 T (B1 0.25 µT, direct sat bandwidth 10.6 Hz ≈ 0.50 ppm): the target at +1.0 ppm is ~21 Hz from water — the direct saturation tail strongly overlaps the target.
  • At 5 T (B1 1.0 µT, bandwidth 42.6 Hz ≈ 0.21 ppm): the offset is ~213 Hz from water — better separation in absolute Hz but the exchange regime is 'intermediate exchange, contrast reduced.' At 7 T (B1 1.5 µT, bandwidth 63.9 Hz ≈ 0.22 ppm): best separation but still constrained by exchange regime.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: The kex of 600 s⁻¹ is borrowed from myo-inositol hydroxyls (PMID 20951217, brain, human in vivo) — not measured for ascorbic acid itself. Ascorbic acid's four distinct OH groups (C2 enolic, C3 enolic, C5/C6 aliphatic) likely have different exchange rates, all lumped into one class value. The myo-inositol rate (600 s⁻¹) is from brain, not pancreas. No pancreas-specific exchange rate exists in the reference table.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.011% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.027% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.068% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=1 µT, Tsat=1000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.162% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=1.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.246% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: For hydroxyl pools at ~1 ppm offset, MTRasym is unreliable because the asymmetry calculation includes direct water saturation. Lorentzian-difference or multi-pool fitting (e.g. 5-pool model: water, MT, amide, amine, hydroxyl) is required to disentangle the hydroxyl CEST effect. The swept B1 of 1.5 µT at 7 T is consistent with intermediate-exchange hydroxyl detection. AREX could remove T1 bias.

hydroxyl CEST (~1.0-1.5 ppm): 1 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). Ascorbic acid has been used as an exogenous CEST contrast agent in tumor models (breast/melanoma, not pancreas). In PDAC, pharmacological ascorbate (high-dose IV vitamin C) is in clinical trials as a therapeutic adjunct. No studies report endogenous ascorbate levels in pancreatic tissue as a disease biomarker. No CEST of endogenous ascorbate in pancreas.

Caveats / critique (5 points, 272 words) — Concentration 7.5 mM ascorbic acid in pancreatic beta cells is reasonable — beta cells accumulate vitamin C via SVCT2 transporters, reaching 7-10 mM. However, t…
  • Concentration 7.5 mM ascorbic acid in pancreatic beta cells is reasonable — beta cells accumulate vitamin C via SVCT2 transporters, reaching 7-10 mM. However, this is intracellular islet concentration, not whole-pancreas average. Concentration varies with nutritional status and between islet vs exocrine tissue.
  • I agree with Agent 2's identification of four exchangeable OH groups classified as 'hydroxyl.' However, a critical error: the simulation treated all four OH groups as identical (shift 1.0 ppm, kex 600 s⁻¹, each at 7.5 mM concentration). This is chemically incorrect. The C3 enolic OH (pKa 4.17) is ~99.94% deprotonated at pH 7.4, carrying effectively zero exchangeable protons.
  • The remaining three OH groups have different chemical environments (C2 enolic vs C5/C6 aliphatic) and likely different exchange rates. The effective CEST-visible concentration is ~2-3 × 7.5 mM, not 4 × 7.5 mM = 30 mM. The simulation overestimates the pool size by ~33-50%. The simulation used 1.0 ppm for all four hydroxyls.
  • EXCI-CEST (PMID 28433532) reported ascorbic acid CEST contrast in the 1-3 ppm range after injection, suggesting a broader or shifted distribution than the single 1.0 ppm value used here. None identified — all four OH groups were listed. However, the C3 enolic OH should arguably be excluded as effectively non-exchangeable at pH 7.4 due to deprotonation.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor This concentration is specific to freshly isolated pancreatic islet cells, not whole pancreas. Each ascorbic acid molecule bears two exchangeable -OH protons (enolic at C2 and C3) that can produce CEST contrast.

Potential clinical impact

broad amide/amine CEST: 1 CEST/NOE application and 1 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 0 animal; 119 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). Only broad pH-sensitive CEST (MTRasym) differentiates PDAC from nontumor pancreas (n=16, AUC 0.857). No CEST study selectively targets the free amino acid pool in the pancreas. Multiple human tissue/serum metabolomics studies (n=51-311 patients) show downregulation of amino acids in PDAC. No animal CEST studies.

Caveats / critique:

  • Concentration 16.4 mM for pooled free amino acids in pancreas is plausible but no specific MRS citation provided. This is a composite pool, not a single molecular species, and concentration varies with nutritional state. Agent 2 correctly identifies alpha-ammonium NH3+ as the sole exchangeable group class ('amine').
  • The assessment that these are in fast exchange producing broad saturation spillover rather than a resolvable CEST peak is sound. No exchangeable protons were neglected. Not simulated: alpha-ammonium NH3+ (pooled across all free amino acids) [amine] -- the reference table has no verified exchange rate and shift for amine protons -- we don't know; not simulated
  • Total free amino acid pool is a summary pool, not a single molecule. Each free amino acid carries one or more exchangeable -NH3+/ -NH2 protons. Individual abundant amino acids from this pool are listed separately below.

Glutamate (free) — CEST: ? unknown (not simulated)

Concentration: 2.50 mM typical (2-4 mM (estimated)) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Total free amino acid pool in rat pancreas = 16.4 mM (PMID 3362844). Glutamate typically constitutes ~15% of total free amino acid pool in soft tissues. 15% of 16.4 = 2.5 mM. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate. In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — Axial, centered on the pancreatic body at the L1 vertebral level (approximately 15-20 mm anterior to the vertebral body).

Why this scan: An axial slice through the upper abdomen at L1 captures pancreas (target), liver, spleen, paraspinal muscle, and renal cortex in one FOV. These tissues have markedly different concentrations of ascorbic acid and glutamine, allowing ROI-differential CEST to separate real metabolite exchange contrast from generic MT/NOE effects. If Z-spectrum differences across ROIs track known concentration gradients, the signal is metabolite-specific.

ROIWhere it is drawnRole
pancreas target tissueEntire pancreatic parenchyma visible on the axial slice, outlined free of peripancreatic fat, excluding the splenic vein and common bile duct if seen. Lobulated T1-intermediate structure in the anterior pararenal space crossing the midline anterior to the aorta and SMA.Target tissue; highest expected ascorbic acid concentration among ROIs (7.5 mM).
liverRight-lobe liver parenchyma drawn centrally away from hepatic vessels and gallbladder fossa. Avoid posterior bare area adjacent to diaphragm.Comparison tissue; moderate ascorbic acid and glutamine content.
spleenSplenic parenchyma in left upper quadrant, drawn centrally to avoid partial-volume from adjacent fat and diaphragm. Homogeneously T2-bright on localizer.Comparison tissue; low ascorbic acid, moderate glutamine.
paraspinal muscleErector spinae or psoas major muscle posteriorly, drawn away from vertebral bone marrow and thecal sac. Uses erector spinae at L1 level.Comparison tissue; very low ascorbic acid, very high glutamine (the largest free glutamine pool in the body).
renal cortexCortical rim of right kidney (more consistently in same axial plane as pancreatic head). Outer 5 mm of renal parenchyma avoiding medullary pyramids.Comparison tissue; low ascorbic acid, low-to-moderate glutamine.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed Gaussian train, B1=1 µT, 40 pulses × 25 ms (interpulse delay 50 ms, duty cycle 33.3%), total Tsat=3000 ms, TR=5000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): At 3 T and 33.3% duty cycle with 1.0 µT peak B1, the average RF power is ~0.33 µT^2-equivalent. For abdominal imaging with a body coil, this is well within FDA/IEC SAR limits (whole-body SAR < 2 W/kg). The long TR (5 s) allows thermal dissipation. Comparable spine and abdominal CEST protocols have been used safely at similar or higher B1.

Compromise rationale: The 1.0 µT, 3 s saturation favors glutamine (physicist's optimum 0.75 µT, 3 s) close to its ideal. For ascorbic acid (optimum 0.75 µT, 750 ms), the 3 s Tsat oversaturates, broadening any narrow hydroxyl peak into the water envelope. The 1.0 µT B1 is 33% above glutamine's optimum but still within the slow-exchange regime for amide protons at 2.2 ppm. A lower B1 (0.5 µT) would under-saturate glutamine; a higher B1 (2 µT) would flood everything into MT spillover.

Fat suppression: SPAIR (SPectral Attenuated Inversion Recovery) fat-suppression prepulse before each saturation train. This axial upper-abdomen slice cuts through visceral and subcutaneous fat (peripancreatic, perirenal, and flank fat). Without suppression, fat protons contribute a direct saturation peak near water that overlaps the hydroxyl offsets (0.8–1.5 ppm). SPAIR at 3 T with TI ~230 ms effectively nulls lipid signal. A water-selective excitation for readout is added as a secondary measure.

Motion mitigation: Respiratory triggering via bellows or navigator on the liver dome. The pancreas and liver move ~10-20 mm craniocaudally during free breathing. A single axial slice at L1 is acquired during end-expiration breath-holds (15-18 s per offset, ~22 offsets = 5-6 min total scan time with 2 min recovery between breath-holds). Alternative: multi-shot EPI with 2-4 shots per offset to fit within a 15 s breath-hold per offset. No cardiac gating needed.

Slice coverage: Single 8-mm axial slice at L1 vertebral body level, centered on the pancreatic body. Alternatively a 3-slice slab (3×6 mm with 1 mm gap) to cover pancreatic head-to-tail while including liver and spleen. Prescribed on a coronal localizer: upper border of L1 to lower border of T12 define the slab's craniocaudal extent.

Structures in FOV: pancreas, liver, spleen, paraspinal muscle, renal cortex, peritoneal fat, vertebral body (bone marrow not directly sampled)

Differential analysis plan:

  • For each ROI, average the Z-spectrum across voxels (excluding outliers >3 SD from mean). Normalize each Z-value to the unsaturated S0 (separate S0 scan). Compute MTRasym = Z(-offset) - Z(+offset) for offsets 0.8, 1.1, 1.3, 1.5 ppm (ascorbic acid) and 2.2 ppm (glutamine).
  • Also compute Lorentzian-difference (LD) spectra by subtracting a 3-pool Lorentzian fit (water + MT + NOE) to isolate residual CEST peaks. Compare MTRasym and LD magnitudes across ROIs using one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD post-hoc. For ascorbic acid: if signal scales pancreas > liver > spleen > renal cortex > muscle (matching concentration rank), this confirms ascorbate-specific CEST.
  • For glutamine: if signal scales paraspinal muscle > liver > spleen > pancreas approx = renal cortex (matching concentration rank), this confirms glutamine-specific CEST. If all ROIs show equal MTRasym at 2.2 ppm despite 5.8x concentration difference between muscle and pancreas, the signal is non-metabolite background (MT/rNOE).
  • For total amino acid pool, glutamate, taurine, and alanine: compare MTRasym at 2.8-3.0 ppm across ROIs — a rank order matching the total amino acid pool concentration (muscle >> liver > spleen > kidney > pancreas) would also be consistent with pooled amine CEST but does not separate individual metabolites.

Not actively targeted:

  • None — all six candidate metabolites have organ_predictions entries. However, total free amino acid pool, glutamate, taurine, and alanine were not actively optimized in the scan protocol because the physicist agent provided empty simulated_contrast_percent_by_field and swept_saturation_by_field fields, meaning no simulation was possible at any field strength.
  • Their exchangeable protons (fast-exchanging alpha-NH3+ at ~2.8-3.0 ppm) are broadened into the water envelope at clinical fields and B1 powers. The Z-spectrum samples at 2.8 and 3.0 ppm are included for exploratory analysis but quantitative predictions are less reliable.
Caveats (6 points, 274 words) — 1. Partial-volume effects: The pancreas is a small structure (2-3 cm thick). At 8 mm slice thickness, peripancreatic fat may contaminate the pancreas ROI. Use h…
  • 1. Partial-volume effects: The pancreas is a small structure (2-3 cm thick). At 8 mm slice thickness, peripancreatic fat may contaminate the pancreas ROI. Use high-resolution anatomical T2-weighted images for ROI delineation. 2. B0 inhomogeneity: The upper abdomen has large susceptibility gradients near bowel gas, lung bases, and vertebral bone.
  • A B0 map (WASSR) at very low power (~0.2 µT, saturation offsets 0 to +1 ppm in 0.1 ppm steps) is essential for voxel-wise correction. 3. B1 inhomogeneity: Body-coil transmission at 3 T has about +/-30% variation across the abdomen. The cest_scout simulation at 0.7x and 1.3x B1 will show robustness. 4. Respiratory motion: The pancreas moves 5-15 mm craniocaudally.
  • Breath-hold acquisitions are required for a single slice — multi-slice or free-breathing approaches will degrade specificity. 5. The single compromise B1 (1.0 µT) and long Tsat (3 s) heavily favor glutamine and likely obliterate any narrow CEST peak from ascorbic acid's fast-exchanging hydroxyl groups, which require much lower B1 and shorter Tsat for detection. 6.
  • Many metabolite concentrations (especially ascorbic acid) lack direct human tissue measurements and rely on textbook estimates or animal data, adding uncertainty to the predicted contrast gradient.
  • [Not simulated] No reference-backed simulation was possible for: pancreas/Total free amino acid pool, liver/Total free amino acid pool, spleen/Total free amino acid pool, paraspinal muscle/Total free amino acid pool, renal cortex/Total free amino acid pool, pancreas/Glutamate (free), liver/Glutamate (free), spleen/Glutamate (free), paraspinal muscle/Glutamate (free), renal cortex/Glutamate (free), pancreas/Taurine (free), liver/Taurine (free), spleen/Taurine (free), paraspinal muscle/Taurine (free), renal cortex/Taurine (free), pancreas/Alanine (free), liver/Alanine (free), spleen/Alanine (free), paraspinal muscle/Alanine (free), renal cortex/Alanine (free).
  • Their predicted_contrast_percent is reported as 0 (not simulated), not as a prediction.
